newsitem.title: UK: Iraqi crude limps into S.Africa after 50-day delay.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi crude limps into S.Africa after 50-day delay.

text.p: One of Iraq's first crude shipments under the United Nations' oil-for-food exchange has arrived in South Africa, more than two months after leaving Iraqi shores, oil traders and shippers said on Friday.

The 272,000 tonne Leonidas, carrying some two million barrels of Iraq's Basrah Light crude, arrived in South Africa's Saldanha Bay late on Thursday night after spending 63 days at sea, normally just a two-week trip.
"I understand the Leonidas arrived in South Africa late last night," said a shipping source.
Caltex, a joint venture between Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc, will refine the cargo at its Cape Town plant having bought the crude on the spot market from Houston-based oil trading outfit Bayoil.
It is South Africa's first and only purchase of Iraqi crude so far under the U.N. plan.

The long-delayed journey illustrates some of the difficulties Baghdad has encountered in resuming exports in the wake of U.N. sanctions which shut down oil sales in August 1990 to punish the invasion of Kuwait.
Iraqi cargoes, hampered by a tough pricing formula into the United States, have failed to find much U.S. buying interest, leaving Europe to soak up most sales.
Bayoil sailed the Leonidas from Iraq's Gulf port Mina al-Bakr on December 19, the second loading from the terminal after the U.N. gave permission for Iraq to resume limited exports.
The tanker suffered engine trouble in the Atlantic on route to its original destination the U.S. Gulf. Mobil Corp, which had bought part of the cargo, cancelled its purchase because of the delay.
The subsequent sale to Caltex was delayed waiting for the U.N. to approve the change of destination into South Africa.
The spot cargo was priced roughly in line with the U.N.'s Dated Brent less $2.15 a barrel for sales to South Africa.
"There was undoubtedly engine trouble but then there was a long delay waiting for approval from the U.N. for a different destination," said a trader.
South Africa looks unlikely to make any immediate extra Iraqi purchases because of sharply declining prices for competing sour crudes.
With oil prices sliding Iraq is having trouble reaching its permitted $1 billion of sales in the first 90 days of the U.N. deal.
Russian lifters in particular have plenty of Iraqi crude to sell.
"We've been offered more. The Russians appear to have plenty," said one South African buyer.
"From a technical point of view it fits but at Brent less $2.15 its too expensive at the moment," he said.
"The price has not been right," said another.
